situation: Block A drives Block B, top-level floorplan gives estimated top interconnect length and launch flop in A, need to write set_input_delay for B in standalone mode
derivation: 1) Get target period T. 2) Estimate launch path: T_launch = T_cq(launch flop in A) + T_comb_top(~20-30% of T for 28nm, ~15% for 7nm) + T_wire_top from Manhattan distance * per-um delay. 3) Add clock skew uncertainty U = 10% T. 4) Input delay = T_launch + U. 5) Leave remainder for B: T_budget_B = T - Input_delay. Example at 1GHz (1ns): T_launch 0.35ns, U 0.1ns => set_input_delay -clock clk 0.45 for B. If B needs more, negotiate.
wrong_way: Setting input delay to 0.5*T as rule-of-thumb or to 0 because 'it will be budgeted later'. First makes B impossible if launch actually 0.6T; second makes B under-constrained and fails at top where launch delay was real, causing top-level setup fails that look like long net but are budget errors.
defense: Show top-level STA sketch with launch flop + estimated wire from PDEF, show that B's remaining budget still allows 12-15 FO4 logic stages; capture screenshot of top-level path before block implementation and log assumption in budget spreadsheet with date.
signoff_risk: Too tight: B over-optimizes, adds area/power, may still pass standalone but creates hold problems and congestion. Too loose: B passes standalone but top-level fails setup by Input_delay error, requires top-level ECO or re-budget late.

situation: Block B drives out to top, need set_output_delay for B's output port
derivation: 1) T required at capture flop in C = T - T_setup_capture - U. 2) Estimate downstream: T_wire_top + T_comb_top to next flop. 3) Output delay = T_wire_top + T_comb_capture_path. Equivalently, output delay = T - (time reserved for B internal to output pin). Typical: T - 0.6T reserved for B => output delay 0.4T. Must be max not min: set_output_delay -max models setup downstream, -min models hold. Derive -min as hold budget: T_hold_capture + U - min wire delay.
wrong_way: Setting output delay to 0 or to T, or copying input delay value. Output delay 0 implies downstream has infinite time, B under-constrains output path; output delay T implies downstream has zero time, B will never close. Both pass block STA but break top.
defense: Show downstream budget sketch, show that B's internal path to port is <0.6T with margin, and that output delay matches top-level timing budget document; run top-level 0-wire estimation with B as black box to verify.
signoff_risk: Too tight: B adds unnecessary buffering on outputs, hurts area, may create DRCs at pins. Too loose: top-level setup fails at capture in C, often misdiagnosed as long interconnect, requires re-budget or B re-implementation.

pattern_name: False path vs multicycle path decision
situation: Control signal like configuration register that changes only on reset or software write, but is in same clock domain as datapath
derivation: 1) Check toggle rate: if signal is static during mission mode and only changes in config mode, candidate for false path. 2) Check if datapath depends on it: if downstream flops are clock-gated or muxed by it and timing would be safe even if late by N cycles, candidate for multicycle. 3) Decision rule: false path only if logical impossibility of simultaneous launch/capture (e.g., mutually exclusive modes). Otherwise use multicycle N. 4) For multicycle N=3, set_multicycle_path N -setup -from <config_reg> -to <all> and N-1 for hold. 5) Add max_delay guard: set_max_delay < N*T for safety.
wrong_way: Marking a slow control as false path because 'it is slow' when it actually can change during active mode. False path removes it from STA entirely, so no delay check, but if it toggles during mission, you get silicon failure with no timing violation. Or using multicycle without adjusting hold, creating hold violation that is hidden.
defense: Show functional spec that config only changes in reset or under software lock, plus CDC-style protocol or simulation trace that config static during active traffic; for multicycle show that functional latency allows N cycles and add assertion that config does not change within N cycles.
signoff_risk: Too tight as false path when should be multicycle: STA passes but silicon fails intermittently because path is real and too slow for single cycle. Too loose as multicycle when true false path: over-constrains block, wastes area/power, but safe. Too loose when false path claimed loose but actually no constraint: chip may fail.

situation: Two clocks are asynchronous (different PLL, different frequency), need to constrain crossing paths without over-constraining synchronous paths
derivation: 1) Identify true async: no phase relationship. 2) Use set_clock_groups -asynchronous -group {clkA} -group {clkB} to cut timing between groups, BUT only for data paths that have explicit synchronizer. 3) For synchronizer chain itself, keep first flop to second flop inside same clock for metastability MTBF, but cut data-to-sync path with set_max_delay -datapath_only. Derivation: max_delay = min(T_A, T_B) - uncertainty, typically 0.6*min period. 4) For handshake, use set_max_delay for req/ack not false path. 5) Never put sync flops in same false path group as data.
wrong_way: Using set_false_path between clocks for all paths because 'async'. That disables both setup and hold and also disables min-delay check for synchronizer, allowing hold failure on sync chain to cause metastability. Or using set_clock_groups -logically_exclusive for async clocks, which is for muxed clocks, not async, and causes incorrect crosstalk and CRPR analysis.
defense: Show synchronizer schematic with 2-flop chain, show that data is stable before req, show protocol timing diagram, and run CDC checker (structural) to prove all crossings have synchronizer; present max_delay report proving crossing meets 0.6T budget.
signoff_risk: Too tight (no exception): impossible timing closure as tool tries to close async path at full rate, leading to over-design. Too loose (false path everywhere): silicon metastability or data incoherency, undetectable in STA, fails in lab under temperature/voltage variation.

situation: Chip IO that interfaces to external device with specified Tco and Tsu, need to constrain input/output without having real clock port inside block
derivation: 1) Create virtual clock: create_clock -name v_clk_ext -period T_ext (same as external device clock, may be same or different from internal). 2) For input: set_input_delay = T_ext - Tsu_ext - board_delay + margin. Example: external device Tco 2ns, board 0.5ns, T=4ns => input_delay = 2.5ns max. 3) For output: set_output_delay = Tsu_ext + board_delay. Add -clock v_clk. 4) Set clock uncertainty between internal clk and v_clk = jitter + board skew 100-200ps. 5) Keep virtual clock not propagated to avoid CTS on it.
wrong_way: Constraining IO directly to internal clock with set_input_delay -clock internal_clk ignoring board delay and external Tco. This double-counts or misses external delay, causing IO paths to appear passing in block but failing at board level, or over-constraining internal logic that shares IO flop.
defense: Show datasheet excerpt of external device Tsu/Tco, board trace length converted to ns, and show that virtual clock period matches external spec not internal; run IO timing report showing external delay included correctly.
signoff_risk: Too tight: internal logic over-buffers to meet IO that actually has more margin, wastes power, may cause hold on input. Too loose: IO fails at system level with external device, requires board rework or chip respin, not caught in chip STA alone.

situation: Block has clock divider (e.g., divide by 2) or muxed clock generating slower clock from fast master, need correct relationship for STA
derivation: 1) Define master: create_clock -period T_master on source pin. 2) Define generated: create_generated_clock -source master_pin -divide_by 2 -master_clock master on divider output. 3) Check -combinational vs sequential: if divider is flop, generated clock latency includes flop cq. 4) Derive uncertainty: generated clock gets extra 30-50ps uncertainty vs master. 5) For paths from master to generated (or vice versa) that are synchronous, tool now knows edge relationship: every 2nd master edge aligns. Do not add false path between them if they are mesochronous. 6) Add set_clock_groups -logically_exclusive only if mux selects one or the other, not both.
wrong_way: Creating two independent create_clock on same net for master and divided clock. STA then treats them as asynchronous with unknown phase, either over-constrains (checks every edge) or under-constrains (misses 2-cycle relationship). Or using set_false_path between master and divided domain to 'fix' failures, hiding real synchronous paths that need 2-cycle budget.
defense: Show clock schematic with divider flop, show generated clock report (report_clocks) showing source and divide, and show timing report that launch on master rising aligns to capture on divided rising with correct 1.5T or 2T budget; provide waveform sketch.
signoff_risk: Too tight (two independent clocks): tool checks 1T instead of 2T for divided domain, impossible closure, over-design. Too loose (false pathed): paths that cross divider domains fail in silicon when phase relationship matters, especially at high freq where 1T vs 2T matters.

situation: Early RTL or floorplan stage, blocks not stable, need SDC that allows implementation to start without final budgets
derivation: 1) Start with 10-15% over-constraint: set_clock period = 0.9*T_target. 2) Add extra uncertainty 100ps at 28nm, 60ps at 7nm. 3) Add set_max_delay 0.85*T on block boundaries. 4) As placement stabilizes and budgets firm up, remove over-constraint in steps: first remove period over-constraint, then reduce uncertainty to 50ps/30ps, then replace max_delay with proper input/output budgets derived from top. 5) Track TNS trend: if TNS improves with over-constraint removed, budget was pessimistic but safe.
wrong_way: Keeping 0.9T over-constraint to signoff because 'more margin is better'. At 28nm this causes 20-30% extra buffers, 15% more area, IR and congestion death; at 7nm causes impossible DRC and power blow-up. Or removing over-constraint too early before floorplan stable, causing ping-pong ECOs.
defense: Show convergence plot: early over-constraint gives early placement with margin, then staged relax with STA reports showing WNS stays positive; justify each relax step with updated top-level budget doc and IR drop check.
signoff_risk: Too tight to end: signoff passes but chip is over-designed, power/area fail spec, may still fail EM/IR due to extra buffers. Too loose too early: late timing surprises 200-300ps after 70% of schedule, requires major rework.

situation: Top-level has Block A -> Block B, both not yet implemented, need to split period between them plus top interconnect
derivation: 1) T_total = T. Reserve top interconnect: T_top = wire_delay_estimate (from floorplan) + 2*buffer delay (~80ps at 28nm, ~40ps at 7nm) + uncertainty U. 2) Remaining T_blocks = T - T_top. 3) Split by complexity: if A has 20 FO4 stages and B has 10, split 66/33, not 50/50. Compute T_A = T_blocks * (stages_A / (stages_A+stages_B)). 4) Add margin 5% to each. 5) Write set_input_delay for B = T_A + T_top/2, set_output_delay for A = T_B + T_top/2. Iterate after first placement.
wrong_way: Always 50/50 split regardless of logic depth, or giving all margin to one block because 'it is harder'. 50/50 on 20-stage vs 5-stage causes easy block to have huge slack and hard block to fail always, leading to endless negotiation; giving all margin to one block hides its inefficiency until top integration.
defense: Show logic depth estimate from synthesis, show floorplan distance and wire delay calc, show that split proportional to FO4 keeps both blocks at ~70% utilization of their budget; document in budget sheet with FO4 count and update after first synth.
signoff_risk: Too tight to A: A fails, requires re-budget late moving margin from B, causes schedule slip. Too loose to both: top-level passes with optimistic budgets but integration fails because sum of actual block delays + top exceeds T by 100-200ps, requires top ECO.
